topics.title: Pronouns, sein and haben
topics.summary: ich, du, er … and the two verbs you need first.

blocks.x: German has a polite **Sie** (always capitalised) for strangers, officials and colleagues, and **du / ihr** for friends, family and children. **sein** (to be) and **haben** (to have) are irregular and appear in almost every sentence, so learn them by heart.
**sie** can mean she, they or (capitalised) polite you. The verb tells you which: sie **ist** = she is, sie **sind** = they are.

topics.title: Present tense
topics.summary: Regular endings, and verbs that change their vowel.

blocks.x: Take the infinitive, drop **-en** and add the ending. The present tense also covers the English future when there is a time word: Morgen **fahre** ich nach Berlin.

Stems ending in **-t** or **-d** add an **e** before -st and -t (du arbeit**e**st). Many strong verbs change their vowel only for **du** and **er/sie/es**: e→i (geben, nehmen), e→ie (lesen, sehen), a→ä (fahren, schlafen).

topics.title: Word order and questions
topics.summary: The verb is always the second element.

blocks.x: In a statement the conjugated verb is in **position 2**. Position 1 can be the subject, a time or place, or an object. If something other than the subject comes first, the subject moves behind the verb.
**W-questions** (wer, was, wo, wann, wie, warum, woher, wohin) keep the verb in position 2. **Yes/no questions** start with the verb.
und, aber, oder, denn and sondern do not count as a position: Ich bin müde, **aber** ich **arbeite** noch.

topics.title: Articles, gender and plural
topics.summary: der, die, das, ein, eine and how plurals are formed.

blocks.x: Every noun is masculine (**der**), feminine (**die**) or neuter (**das**). Learn each noun together with its article and plural. In the plural the article is always **die**, whatever the gender.

Common plural patterns: **-e** (Tisch → Tische), **-(e)n** (Lampe → Lampen, most feminine nouns), **-er** with umlaut (Buch → Bücher), **-s** (Auto → Autos, loan words), and no ending (Lehrer → Lehrer).
Endings often give the gender away: -ung, -heit, -keit are die; -chen is das. The Der Die Das tab lists the rules and quizzes you.

topics.title: Accusative
topics.summary: The direct object: only der changes, to den.

blocks.x: The subject is in the nominative, the direct object in the **accusative**. Only the masculine changes: **der → den, ein → einen, kein → keinen**. Feminine, neuter and plural stay the same.

Verbs like haben, brauchen, kaufen, sehen, suchen, essen, trinken and es gibt take the accusative. Pronouns: ich → **mich**, du → **dich**, er → **ihn**, wir → **uns**, ihr → **euch**, sie/Sie → **sie/Sie**.

topics.title: Negation: nicht or kein
topics.summary: kein for nouns with ein or no article, nicht for everything else.

blocks.x: Use **kein** to negate a noun that would have **ein** or no article. It takes the same endings as ein. Use **nicht** for verbs, adjectives, adverbs and nouns with der/die/das or a possessive.
nicht usually goes to the end of the sentence, but before adjectives, places and the second part of the verb: Ich bin **nicht** müde. Er ist **nicht** gekommen.

topics.title: Modal verbs
topics.summary: können, müssen, wollen, dürfen, sollen, möchten.

blocks.x: The modal verb is conjugated in position 2, and the second verb goes to the **end** in the infinitive. ich and er/sie/es have the same form and no ending.

x: You have to get up early tomorrow.
You're not allowed to smoke here.
I'd like to order a coffee.

blocks.x: **nicht müssen** means 'don't have to', not 'mustn't': Du musst nicht kommen = you don't have to come. 'Mustn't' is **nicht dürfen**.

topics.title: Separable verbs
topics.summary: anrufen → Ich rufe dich an.

blocks.x: Verbs with a stressed prefix such as **an-, auf-, aus-, ein-, mit-, vor-, zu-, fern-** split in the present and past: the main part goes to position 2, the prefix to the **end**. With a modal verb, or at the end of a subordinate clause, they stay together.
be-, ge-, er-, ver-, zer-, ent-, emp- and miss- never separate: Ich **verstehe** dich. Ich **bekomme** ein Paket.

topics.title: Possessive articles
topics.summary: mein, dein, sein, ihr, unser, euer, Ihr.

blocks.x: Possessives take the same endings as **ein / kein**. Choose the word by the owner, and the ending by the noun that follows.

topics.title: Imperative
topics.summary: Giving instructions: Komm! Kommt! Kommen Sie!

blocks.x: The **du** form is the du-present without **-st** and without du (du nimmst → Nimm!). Verbs that change a → ä do not keep the umlaut: du fährst → **Fahr!** Add **bitte** or **doch mal** to sound friendlier.

topics.title: Perfect tense
topics.summary: How you talk about the past: haben/sein + participle.

blocks.x: In speech, the past is almost always the **Perfekt**: **haben** or **sein** in position 2, the **past participle** at the end.

Use **sein** with verbs of movement from A to B (gehen, fahren, fliegen, kommen) and change of state (aufstehen, einschlafen, sterben), plus sein, bleiben and passieren. Everything else uses **haben**.

x: Have you done the shopping yet?

topics.title: Dative
topics.summary: The indirect object: dem, der, dem, den …n.

blocks.x: The **dative** marks the person who receives something (the indirect object), and follows certain verbs and prepositions.

Pronouns: mir, dir, ihm, ihr, ihm, uns, euch, ihnen, **Ihnen**. Verbs with the dative: helfen, danken, gefallen, gehören, schmecken, passen, antworten, gratulieren. In the plural the noun adds **-n**: mit den Kinder**n**.

x: Ich gebe dem Kind einen Apfel.
I give the child an apple.

topics.title: Prepositions and cases
topics.summary: Which prepositions take accusative, dative or both.

head: Case
Prepositions
rows: aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von, zu, gegenüber
an, auf, hinter, in, neben, über, unter, vor, zwischen

blocks.x: Two-way prepositions take the **accusative for movement to a place** (Wohin?) and the **dative for location** (Wo?). Common contractions: in dem → **im**, an dem → **am**, zu dem → **zum**, zu der → **zur**, in das → **ins**, bei dem → **beim**.

x: Ich lege das Buch auf den Tisch.
I put the book on the table. (where to → accusative)
Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch.
The book is on the table. (where → dative)
Er fährt mit dem Bus zur Arbeit.
He takes the bus to work.

topics.title: Past of sein, haben and modals
topics.summary: Even in speech these use the simple past.

blocks.x: For sein, haben and modal verbs Germans use the **Präteritum**, not the Perfekt, also when speaking. ich and er/sie/es have the same form.

topics.title: Subordinate clauses: weil, dass, wenn
topics.summary: The conjugated verb goes to the end.

blocks.x: After **weil** (because), **dass** (that), **wenn** (if, whenever), **ob** (whether) and question words in indirect questions, the conjugated verb moves to the **end** of the clause. A comma separates the clauses.

x: Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich krank bin.
I'm staying at home because I'm ill.
Ich glaube, dass er morgen kommt.
Wenn es regnet, fahren wir mit dem Bus.
If it rains, we'll take the bus.
Weißt du, wann der Zug ankommt?
Do you know when the train arrives?

blocks.x: If the subordinate clause comes first, it counts as position 1, so the main clause **starts with the verb**: Wenn es regnet, **fahren** wir … Separable verbs join up at the end: …, dass er um 7 **aufsteht**.
**denn** also means because, but it is not a subordinating word, so the verb stays in position 2: Ich bleibe zu Hause, **denn** ich **bin** krank.

topics.title: Comparing: comparative and superlative
topics.summary: schnell, schneller, am schnellsten.

blocks.x: Use **als** for 'than' and **so … wie** for 'as … as'. Many short adjectives take an umlaut (alt → älter, jung → jünger).

x: Mein Bruder ist so alt wie du.
My brother is as old as you.
Im Sommer ist es hier am schönsten.

topics.title: Reflexive verbs
topics.summary: sich freuen, sich waschen, sich treffen.

blocks.x: Reflexive verbs need a pronoun that refers back to the subject. It is the same as the accusative pronoun except for **sich** (er, sie, es, sie, Sie).

x: Ich freue mich auf den Urlaub.
I'm looking forward to the holiday.

blocks.x: With a direct object the pronoun is dative: Ich wasche **mich**, but Ich wasche **mir** die Hände.

topics.title: Adjective endings
topics.summary: der neue Tisch, ein neuer Tisch, neuer Tisch.

blocks.x: An adjective after **is** or **bleibt** has no ending (Der Tisch ist neu). Before a noun it needs one. After **der/die/das** the ending is only ever **-e** or **-en**: -e in the nominative singular and in the feminine and neuter accusative, -en everywhere else.
Where ein has no ending of its own (ein Tisch, ein Bett), the adjective shows the gender instead: ein neu**er** Tisch, ein neu**es** Bett.

topics.title: Simple past
topics.summary: The written past tense used in stories and news.

blocks.x: In writing (books, news, reports) the past is usually the **Präteritum**. Regular verbs add **-te**; irregular verbs change their stem and have no ending for ich and er/sie/es.

x: Once upon a time there was a king.
Er öffnete die Tür und ging hinaus.
He opened the door and went out.

blocks.x: The Verben tab shows the Präteritum for every verb and marks irregular forms in colour.

topics.title: Relative clauses
topics.summary: Der Mann, der dort steht …

blocks.x: A relative clause describes a noun. The relative pronoun takes its **gender and number from the noun** and its **case from its role in the relative clause**. The verb goes to the end.

x: Der Mann, der dort steht, ist mein Chef.
The man who is standing there is my boss.
Das ist der Film, den ich gestern gesehen habe.
That's the film (that) I saw yesterday.
Die Kollegin, mit der ich arbeite, ist nett.
The colleague I work with is nice.
Die Kinder, denen wir geholfen haben, …

blocks.x: Unlike English, the relative pronoun can never be left out, and a preposition always goes in front of it: mit **der**, für **den**.

topics.title: Passive
topics.summary: werden + participle: Das Haus wird gebaut.

blocks.x: The passive puts the action in focus rather than who does it. Use **werden** + past participle. The doer, if needed, follows **von** + dative.

x: Der Brief wurde von meiner Chefin geschrieben.
The letter was written by my boss.

blocks.x: In the passive Perfekt the participle of werden is **worden**, not geworden.

topics.title: Konjunktiv II: wishes and politeness
topics.summary: würde, hätte, wäre, könnte.

blocks.x: The Konjunktiv II expresses wishes, unreal conditions, advice and polite requests. Most verbs use **würde + infinitive**; sein, haben and the modals have their own forms.

x: Wenn ich Zeit hätte, würde ich mitkommen.
If I had time, I would come along.
I'd love to be at the seaside.
An deiner Stelle würde ich zum Arzt gehen.
If I were you, I'd see a doctor.

topics.title: Genitive
topics.summary: des Mannes, der Frau, wegen des Wetters.

blocks.x: The **genitive** shows possession and follows a few prepositions. Masculine and neuter nouns add **-s** or **-es**. In speech it is often replaced by **von** + dative.
Prepositions with the genitive: **wegen** (because of), **trotz** (despite), **während** (during), **statt** (instead of), **innerhalb / außerhalb** (inside / outside).

x: Das ist das Auto meines Vaters.
Wegen des Regens bleiben wir zu Hause.
Because of the rain, we're staying at home.
Während der Woche arbeite ich viel.
I work a lot during the week.

blocks.x: Names take -s without an apostrophe: **Annas** Bruder, not Anna's.

topics.title: Infinitive with zu, um … zu
topics.summary: Ich habe keine Lust, heute zu kochen.

blocks.x: After many verbs and expressions (versuchen, vergessen, anfangen, aufhören, Lust/Zeit haben, es ist wichtig/schwer) the second verb goes to the end with **zu**. Separable verbs put zu in the middle: an**zu**rufen.

x: Es ist wichtig, genug zu schlafen.
It's important to get enough sleep.
Hast du Lust, ins Kino zu gehen?
Do you fancy going to the cinema?

blocks.x: **um … zu** gives the purpose (in order to) when the subject is the same in both parts. With different subjects use **damit**.

x: Ich lerne Deutsch, um in Deutschland zu arbeiten.
I'm learning German in order to work in Germany.
Ich spreche langsam, damit du mich verstehst.
I speak slowly so that you understand me.

blocks.x: Modal verbs never take zu: Ich **kann** schwimmen, not ich kann zu schwimmen.

topics.title: Linking words
topics.summary: obwohl, trotzdem, deshalb, als, nachdem and pairs.

head: Type
Words
Verb position
rows: obwohl, als, nachdem, bevor, während, seit, bis, falls, sodass
trotzdem, deshalb, deswegen, dann, danach, sonst

x: Obwohl es regnet, gehen wir spazieren.
Although it's raining, we're going for a walk.
Es regnet. Trotzdem gehen wir spazieren.
It's raining. We're going for a walk anyway.
Ich war müde, deshalb bin ich früh ins Bett gegangen.
I was tired, so I went to bed early.
Als ich ein Kind war, wohnte ich in Köln.
When I was a child, I lived in Cologne.

blocks.x: **als** is for a single event or period in the past; **wenn** is for the present, the future and repeated events (immer wenn). Two-part connectors: **sowohl … als auch** (both … and), **entweder … oder** (either … or), **weder … noch** (neither … nor), **nicht nur … sondern auch** (not only … but also).

x: Ich spreche sowohl Englisch als auch Deutsch.
I speak both English and German.
Wir fahren entweder nach Italien oder nach Spanien.
We're going either to Italy or to Spain.

topics.title: Future
topics.summary: werden + infinitive, for plans, promises and guesses.

blocks.x: Most of the time Germans use the present tense with a time word for the future. **werden + infinitive** is used for promises, predictions and guesses about the present.
Don't confuse it with English 'want': **ich will** = I want to; **ich werde** = I will.
